# The Barbarian's Morning

## A Novel

---

### Chapter I: Awakening in Marble Halls

The first pale fingers of dawn crept through the latticed windows of the imperial villa on the Palatine Hill, casting geometric patterns of gold and shadow across the mosaic floor. The tiny tessellated tiles — depicting Bacchus in his chariot, surrounded by cavorting satyrs and trailing grapevines — glimmered faintly as the morning light touched their glazed surfaces one by one, as if the god of wine himself were slowly waking from his eternal revelry.

Upon the enormous sleeping couch, draped in Tyrian purple silks and the softest Egyptian linens, a figure stirred. He was not Roman. That much was immediately apparent from the sheer size of him — the way his long legs extended nearly to the foot of the oversized lectus, the way his broad shoulders consumed more than their rightful share of the embroidered bolster cushions. He was a creature of the forests, of the cold rivers and vast twilight woodlands beyond the Rhine, and even in sleep, even wrapped in the decadent fabrics of empire, there was something untamed about him — something that no amount of perfumed oil or fine linen could fully domesticate.

His name was Wulfgar, son of Sigeric, of the Cherusci tribe, and he was twenty winters old.

He had come to Rome not in chains, as so many of his kinsmen had, dragged behind triumphant chariots for the amusement of the howling mob. No — Wulfgar had come willingly, though the circumstances of his arrival were as complicated and tangled as the knotwork patterns his mother had once embroidered on his childhood tunics. He had been part of a diplomatic exchange, one of several young Germanic nobles sent to the imperial court as a gesture of good faith following the latest round of treaties along the northern frontier. He was meant to be a hostage, technically — a living guarantee of his tribe's continued cooperation with Rome.

But Emperor Hadrian — or rather, Publius Aelius Hadrianus Augustus, as the Romans insisted on calling him with their endless multiplication of names — had taken one look at the young Germanic warrior upon his arrival at court and had seen something more than a political pawn. What exactly the emperor had seen, Wulfgar still was not entirely certain, even after six months of living in the imperial residence, eating from golden plates, bathing in heated pools, and sharing the emperor's bed.

*Perhaps he sees in me what he sees in his Greek statues,* Wulfgar thought drowsily, his mind swimming up slowly from the depths of sleep like a trout rising toward the surface of a still pool. *Something beautiful. Something wild. Something he can look at and admire but never truly possess.*

He opened his eyes.

The ceiling above him was painted with an elaborate fresco — Aurora, goddess of the dawn, driving her rose-colored chariot across a sky of lapis lazuli blue, scattering flowers before her as she went. The artist had been extraordinarily skilled; the goddess's robes billowed with such convincing motion that they seemed to ripple in an unseen wind, and the horses that drew her chariot appeared to strain and leap with genuine muscular effort. Wulfgar had spent many mornings staring up at this ceiling, and he had decided that while the Romans were soft, decadent, and overly fond of talking, they were without question masters of making beautiful things.

*My people paint ourselves blue and carve faces into trees,* he mused, blinking sleep from his eyes. *These Romans paint the heavens on their ceilings. Perhaps there is something to be said for civilization after all.*

He turned his head on the pillow and found the space beside him empty. The emperor had already risen, as was his habit — Hadrian was a man of rigorous discipline despite his love of art and beauty, and he typically rose before dawn to attend to matters of state, review correspondence from the provinces, and meet with his consilium of advisors. The sheets on his side of the bed were cool to the touch, suggesting he had been gone for some time.

Wulfgar stretched luxuriously, his massive frame expanding across the bed like a cat unfurling in a patch of sunlight. His joints popped and crackled — a series of satisfying little detonations that traveled from his shoulders down through his spine to his hips. The sound reminded him of green wood crackling in a campfire, and for a fleeting moment, a pang of homesickness lanced through his chest — sharp and bright and quickly suppressed.

*No,* he told himself firmly. *Do not think of home this morning. Think of here. Think of now. Think of what the day holds.*

He lay still for another moment, luxuriating in the absurd comfort of the bed. In his homeland, he had slept on a pallet of straw and furs on the hard-packed earthen floor of his father's longhouse, with the smoke of the central hearth stinging his eyes and the sound of livestock shifting and lowing just beyond the partition wall. Here, the mattress beneath him was stuffed with the finest wool from Tarantine sheep, the pillows filled with goose down, and the air was perfumed with traces of the sandalwood and myrrh incense that the household slaves burned each evening in bronze censers shaped like crouching lions.

*Sigeric, my father, would spit on this softness,* Wulfgar thought, and the corners of his mouth twitched upward in a private smile. *He would say it makes a man weak. That a warrior should sleep on stone and eat raw meat and never know comfort, lest comfort dull his blade and slow his arm.*

But Sigeric was far away, beyond the Rhine, beyond the dark forests and the cold marshes, in a world that felt increasingly like something Wulfgar had dreamed rather than lived. And this — this villa with its marble columns and painted ceilings and heated floors and impossible luxuries — this was real. This was now.

*And besides,* he added to himself, swinging his legs over the edge of the bed and planting his bare feet on the cool mosaic floor, *Father never had the opportunity to sleep on Tarantine wool. If he had, he might feel differently about the virtues of stone.*

He stood.

The morning air was cool against his skin — he had slept in only a light linen subligaculum, the Roman undergarment that he had reluctantly adopted after his first week at court, when it had been gently explained to him that wandering the imperial palace in nothing but a wolf-skin loincloth was causing distress among the household staff. The garment was wrapped loosely around his hips, and as he stood, it shifted and sagged, threatening to slip free entirely.

Wulfgar padded across the bedroom floor toward the large bronze mirror that stood in the corner of the room, mounted on an ornate stand carved to resemble a pair of intertwined dolphins. The mirror was one of Hadrian's many gifts — the emperor was perpetually showering him with presents, as if beautiful objects could serve as a language when words failed to bridge the gap between their two worlds. Wulfgar had received jewelry, clothing, weapons, books (which he could not read, though he was learning), a magnificent white stallion from Hispania, and this mirror, which was polished to such a perfect sheen that it reflected his image with almost supernatural clarity.

He stopped before it and regarded himself.

*The Romans think I am beautiful,* he thought, studying his reflection with the frank, unselfconscious appraisal of a man who had grown up in a culture where vanity was not considered a vice but simply an honest acknowledgment of the gods' gifts. *Hadrian tells me so every night, in that soft voice he uses when we are alone, when the emperor falls away and the man emerges. He says I look like something carved from northern ice. He says my eyes are the color of the sky above the German forests. He says—*

He shook his head, scattering the thoughts like startled birds.

*Enough. You are not some Roman maiden to stand before a mirror cataloguing compliments. You are Wulfgar, son of Sigeric, of the Cherusci. Act like it.*

But still, he lingered before the mirror for another moment, because the truth was that even after six months in Rome, the sight of himself still struck him as faintly foreign — as if the young man reflected in the polished bronze were a stranger he was only gradually getting to know.

The villa was quiet. Beyond the bedroom, Wulfgar could hear the distant sounds of the household beginning its daily rhythm — the murmur of slaves' voices, the clatter of pottery in the kitchens, the soft shuffling of sandaled feet on stone corridors. But this wing of the villa, the private apartments that Hadrian reserved for himself and his most intimate companions, was hushed and still, a pocket of silence within the larger bustle of the imperial residence.

*The pond,* Wulfgar thought suddenly, and the idea struck him with the force of revelation, as if some benevolent forest spirit had whispered it directly into his ear. *I will go to the pond.*

The pond in question was a large ornamental pool situated in the villa's expansive gardens — a kidney-shaped body of water fed by a natural spring and surrounded by carefully tended cypress trees, flowering oleander bushes, and beds of lavender that perfumed the air with their sweet, herbaceous scent. Hadrian had stocked it with fish — fat, lazy carp and quick silver dace — purely for aesthetic purposes, because the Romans apparently believed that even their water features should be populated with beautiful living things. Wulfgar had discovered the pond during his first week at the villa, and it had immediately become his favorite place on the entire estate.

It reminded him of home. Not precisely — the water was too warm, the surrounding vegetation too manicured, the whole scene too artfully composed to truly resemble the wild forest pools of his childhood. But there was something about the quality of the light on the water in the early morning, something about the way the fish moved in the green depths like living flickers of silver and gold, that called to a deep and primal part of his soul. When he sat beside the pond, or better yet immersed himself in it, he felt a connection to something older and more fundamental than Rome, older even than his own tribe — a connection to the water itself, to the ancient and sacred element that his people revered as the dwelling place of spirits and the source of all life.

*Yes,* he decided firmly. *The pond. Now. Before the slaves come with their towels and their oil flasks and their endless fussing.*

He moved toward the door of the bedroom, then paused and looked down at himself — at the linen subligaculum riding low on his hips, at his bare chest and bare feet.

*I could dress properly,* he thought. *I could put on a tunic, sandals. I could walk through the gardens like a civilized man, like a Roman, and arrive at the pond fully clothed, and then undress carefully, folding each garment and setting it aside, as Hadrian does when he prepares for the baths.*

The thought lasted approximately two heartbeats.

*Or I could not.*

A grin spread across his face — the wide, uncomplicated grin of a young man who has remembered, however briefly, that he is young, and that the morning is new, and that there is a cool pond waiting for him in a garden full of flowers.

He reached down, hooked his thumbs under the waistband of the subligaculum, and pushed it down over his hips. The linen garment slithered down his thighs, past his knees, and pooled around his ankles. He stepped out of it, kicked it carelessly aside, and stood completely, utterly, magnificently naked.

---

### Chapter II: The Barbarian Unclothed

Wulfgar stood before the bronze mirror one final time, and now the reflection that gazed back at him was stripped of all Roman artifice, all civilized pretension. What remained was the essential creature — the young Germanic warrior in his most natural and unadorned state.

His skin was extraordinarily white — not the pallid, unhealthy white of a man who had spent too long indoors, but a luminous, almost incandescent white, the color of fresh cream or new snow or the inner bark of a birch tree. It was the complexion of the far north, bred into his bloodline over countless generations of long winters and pale sunlight, and it seemed almost to glow in the soft morning light that filtered through the latticed windows. The Roman sun had not yet managed to significantly alter this fundamental fairness, though six months of Mediterranean climate had laid the faintest wash of gold across his shoulders and the bridge of his nose, like a watercolor artist's most tentative first stroke.

His face was striking rather than classically handsome — at least by Roman standards, which favored the clean, symmetrical proportions exemplified by their Greek-inspired statuary. His features were bold, emphatic, almost aggressive in their distinctiveness. His jaw was strong and square, shaded with the pale golden stubble of a day's growth; his cheekbones were high and prominent, casting shadows beneath them that gave his face a sculpted, angular quality. His nose was straight and well-formed but slightly too large by Roman tastes — a proud, assertive nose that announced itself unapologetically upon the landscape of his face. His lips were full and surprisingly soft-looking for such an otherwise rugged countenance, their natural color a deep rose-pink that the emperor had once compared, in a moment of drowsy post-coital poetry, to the wild roses that grew along the banks of the Tiber in spring.

But it was his eyes that arrested attention and held it. They were large, wide-set, and of a blue so pale and clear and penetrating that they seemed almost to emit light rather than merely reflect it. They were the blue of glacier melt, of winter sky, of the translucent ice that formed on the surface of still ponds in the deepest cold of a Germanic January. There was something startling about those eyes — something that made people look twice, that made even jaded Roman courtiers pause mid-sentence and momentarily lose their train of thought. Hadrian had once told him that looking into his eyes was like looking through a window into the wild north itself, and Wulfgar had not known whether to take this as a compliment or an observation.

His hair was a wonder. It fell to just past his shoulders in a thick, heavy cascade the color of ripe wheat — a deep, warm gold that lightened almost to silver-white at the temples and the very tips, where the sun had bleached it. It was the kind of hair that Roman women would have killed for and Roman men secretly envied — thick and lustrous and alive with a natural wave that gave it movement and body, so that it shifted and rippled with even the slightest turn of his head, catching the light and releasing it in little flashes of gold. This morning it was tousled and wild from sleep, hanging in disorderly curtains around his face, with several strands falling across his forehead and one persistent lock curling behind his left ear. He made no move to tame it. Combs and brushes were Roman inventions, as far as he was concerned, and his hair had survived twenty years without their intervention.

*Hadrian loves my hair,* he thought, absently running his fingers through the tangled mass, working out the worst of the knots with a practiced, unconscious motion. *He loves to touch it, to bury his face in it, to wrap it around his fingers. He says it smells of pine forests and wood smoke, even after the slaves have washed it with their perfumed soaps. He says it reminds him that I am not Roman, that I come from a place where the world is still wild and new.*

His gaze traveled downward, tracing the lines of his own body with an almost clinical detachment.

His neck was thick and corded with muscle — the neck of a man who had spent his adolescence wrestling, fighting, and carrying heavy loads through difficult terrain. It flowed into broad, square shoulders that seemed almost impossibly wide for his age, their breadth accentuated by the prominent ridges of his trapezius muscles, which rose on either side of his neck like the roots of a great tree. His collarbones were sharp and well-defined, creating deep hollows at the base of his throat where shadows gathered.

His chest was a masterwork of natural architecture. It was broad and deep, built for the expansion of powerful lungs, and the two great slabs of his pectoral muscles were thick and solid, with a definition that came not from the calculated exercises of the Roman gymnasium but from years of genuine physical labor and martial training — from swinging axes, drawing longbows, paddling canoes against strong river currents, and engaging in the brutal, full-contact wrestling that was the Cherusci's favorite pastime. A dusting of fine golden hair covered his chest, thicker at the center where a narrow trail led down across the corrugated surface of his abdomen. This hair was soft and almost invisible in certain lights, but in the warm glow of the morning sun, it caught the light and turned to spun gold, giving his chest a subtle, warm radiance.

His stomach was flat and hard, ribbed with the stacked blocks of abdominal muscle that the Romans admired so much in their depictions of gods and heroes. The muscles were clearly defined but not ostentatiously so — they were the functional muscles of a working body, not the artificially cultivated ones of a man who spent his days in the gymnasium lifting weights for aesthetic purposes. A thin line of golden hair ran from his navel downward, darkening slightly as it descended, like a trail leading into a forest.

His arms were perhaps his most impressive feature from a purely physical standpoint. They were long, thick, and roped with muscle, the product of years of weapons training that had begun when he was barely old enough to grip a sword hilt. His biceps were round and full, bunching prominently even at rest, and his forearms were dense and corded, etched with veins that stood out beneath the pale skin like the rivers on a Roman map. His hands were large, broad-palmed, and callused, with thick, strong fingers — hands that had been made for gripping weapons, for tearing, for building, for all the rough and necessary work of survival in a world without servants and slaves. The contrast between these rough, powerful hands and the delicate luxury of the imperial villa in which they now found themselves was one of the many small ironies of Wulfgar's current existence.

As he turned slightly in the mirror, his back came into view — a broad, muscular expanse that tapered from his wide shoulders down to a narrow waist in a dramatic V-shape. The muscles of his back were complex and layered, shifting beneath his pale skin like tectonic plates as he moved, and the deep groove of his spine ran down the center like a river valley between two mountain ranges.

And then there was his backside.

Wulfgar's buttocks were, to put it plainly, magnificent. They were two full, round, powerfully muscled globes that projected prominently from the base of his spine, high and firm and shapely, with a density and solidity that spoke of thousands of miles walked, hundreds of hills climbed, countless hours spent in the saddle and in the wrestler's crouch. They were the buttocks of a young man in the absolute prime of his physical existence — taut and smooth and pale as marble, unmarked by any blemish, dimpling slightly at the sides when he flexed, which he did now, unconsciously, as he shifted his weight from one foot to the other. A fine, almost invisible layer of golden down covered their curved surfaces, visible only when the light caught it at precisely the right angle, and the deep cleft between them was shadowed and private, a hidden valley between two snow-white hills.

Now, it must be said — and here we must speak frankly, for this is a story about a barbarian, and barbarians are nothing if not frank — that Wulfgar, standing naked in the warm morning air after a full night's sleep, was not what one might call freshly bathed. The Romans were obsessed with bathing, it was true, and their elaborate bath complexes with their heated pools and cold plunges and armies of attendants armed with strigils and oil flasks were among the genuinely impressive achievements of their civilization. But Wulfgar had been asleep for many hours, tangled in warm linens, and his body had done what all healthy young bodies do during the night — it had perspired, it had metabolized, it had carried on the quiet, ceaseless business of being alive.

The result was that the young barbarian, in his current unclothed state, carried with him the honest, potent scent of his own physicality. His armpits — deep, hollow cavities framed by the thick muscles of his chest and shoulders and thatched with dense bushes of dark golden hair several shades deeper than the hair on his head — radiated a powerful, musky aroma that was equal parts sharp and sweet. It was the smell of healthy young male exertion concentrated and fermented through a night of warm sleep — a dense, loamy, almost animalic scent that had distinct notes of raw onion, fresh-cut oak, and something darker and more primal beneath, something that belonged to the world of forests and earth and rutting stags. It was not an unpleasant smell, exactly — or rather, it was the kind of smell whose pleasantness or unpleasantness depended entirely on one's perspective. A Roman senator might have recoiled. Hadrian, Wulfgar knew from intimate experience, would have buried his face in those golden-thatched hollows and breathed deep, because the emperor had confessed on more than one occasion that Wulfgar's natural scent intoxicated him more than any perfume.

The cleft of his buttocks told a similar olfactory story, though in a different register. Here, the scent was earthier, deeper, more concentrated — the rich, humid funk of a warm, enclosed space that had been pressed between mattress and body for the better part of eight hours. It was a ripe, pungent, unmistakably organic smell, dense and mushroomy, with a biting, ammoniac edge that spoke of the body's most fundamental biological processes. The golden hairs that lightly lined the crevice held and concentrated this scent, trapping it in a fragrant pocket of warmth, so that any movement — any shift of his hips, any flex of those powerful gluteal muscles — released a fresh wave of concentrated musk into the surrounding air.

Wulfgar was entirely unconscious of these scents, or rather, he was so accustomed to them that they registered no more on his awareness than the sound of his own breathing. In the world he came from, the world beyond the Rhine, bodies smelled like bodies, and that was simply the way of things. The Roman obsession with masking and eliminating natural odors through perfumes, oils, and compulsive bathing struck him as bizarre at best and suspicious at worst — as if the Romans were trying to hide something, to disguise some fundamental truth about themselves that they found shameful.

*I smell like a man,* he thought, catching a faint whiff of himself as he raised his arm to push his hair back from his face. *Like a living, breathing man. There is no shame in that. The gods made us to smell as we smell, and I will not apologize for it.*

He gave himself one final appraising look in the mirror — the long, lean, white-skinned body with its golden hair and ice-blue eyes, its powerful muscles and bold features, standing naked and unashamed in the morning light of an emperor's bedroom — and he nodded once, satisfied.

*Not bad, for a barbarian.*

Then he turned, crossed the room in three long strides, and slipped through the doorway into the corridor beyond, as naked as the day his mother had brought him howling into the world in a smoke-filled longhouse beside the river Weser, twenty years and a lifetime ago.

---

### Chapter III: The Garden Path

The corridor was empty, which was a small mercy, though Wulfgar would not have been particularly perturbed if it hadn't been. The household slaves were accustomed to his habits by now — his casual relationship with clothing, his tendency to wander the villa in various states of undress, his apparent inability to understand (or his willful refusal to acknowledge) the elaborate Roman codes of modesty and propriety that governed the wearing of garments in different social contexts. In his first weeks at the villa, his nude perambulations had caused considerable consternation among the staff, but Hadrian had intervened with characteristic pragmatism, issuing a quiet instruction that the barbarian was to be left to his own devices in matters of personal attire, and that anyone who found the sight of an unclothed Germanic warrior offensive was welcome to look elsewhere.

The stone floor was cool beneath Wulfgar's bare feet as he padded down the corridor, and he savored the sensation — the smooth, slightly gritty texture of the marble against his soles, the chill that crept up through the bones of his feet and into his ankles. The corridor was lined with niches containing marble busts of various Roman worthies — emperors, generals, philosophers, their blank stone eyes gazing out with expressions of studied nobility — and Wulfgar passed them without a glance. He had given them all names during his first week: that one with the laurel wreath was "Old Sour-Face"; the one with the heroically jutting chin was "The Jaw"; the one at the far end, whose sculptor had given him an expression of vague, beneficent surprise, was "The Man Who Sat on a Hedgehog."

*Good morning, Hedgehog Man,* Wulfgar thought as he passed the last bust and turned the corner toward the garden entrance. *I trust you slept as well as I did. Though with that expression, perhaps not.*

He reached the large double doors that led from the villa's interior to the garden terrace. They were made of dark, heavy wood — Lebanese cedar, he had been told, imported at fantastic expense — and they were standing slightly ajar, propped open to admit the morning air. Wulfgar pushed through them and stepped outside.

The impact was immediate and glorious.

The morning air hit his naked body like a benediction — cool and fresh and sweet, carrying with it the mingled fragrances of the garden's thousand growing things. Lavender, rosemary, jasmine, oleander, the deep green scent of cypress and the lighter, more playful perfume of orange blossom — they swirled around him in a fragrant symphony that made his nostrils flare and his chest expand involuntarily with a deep, appreciative breath. The sky above was the pale, luminous blue of early morning — not yet the deep, saturated cobalt it would become later in the day, but a delicate, watery shade that reminded him of the inside of a robin's egg.

*This,* he thought, spreading his arms wide and tilting his face up toward the rising sun, letting the light fall on his closed eyelids and paint the inside of his vision with warm orange, *this is what I come outside for. Not the marble. Not the mosaics. This. The air. The light. The feeling of being alive in a world that is alive around me.*

The garden terrace was a broad, paved expanse of pale travertine stone, bordered by low walls topped with terracotta pots overflowing with trailing geraniums and cascading ivy. Beyond the terrace, the garden proper spread out in an elaborate geometric design — gravel paths, clipped hedges, flowerbeds, ornamental trees, fountains, and statuary — all arranged with the precise, almost mathematical orderliness that the Romans brought to everything they did, from their road-building to their lovemaking.

Wulfgar descended the terrace steps — three broad, shallow stairs — and his bare feet met the gravel of the garden path. The stones were small and smooth, sun-warmed already despite the early hour, and they crunched softly beneath his weight as he began to walk.

He was aware, as he walked, of the picture he must present — a tall, naked, golden-haired barbarian striding through the manicured gardens of a Roman emperor's villa, his long hair streaming behind him, his pale skin almost phosphorescent in the early light, his every stride revealing and concealing the powerful musculature of his legs and the prominent flex of his bare buttocks. He imagined what one of the garden slaves would think if they happened to glance up from their pruning and see him — this apparition of northern wildness moving through the ordered Roman landscape like a wolf through a sheep pen.

*They would probably drop their shears,* he thought, and smiled.

The path wound through a grove of ancient olive trees, their gnarled silver trunks twisted into fantastic shapes by centuries of growth, their leaves rustling with a dry, whispering sound in the faint morning breeze. Beyond the olive grove, the path curved around a bed of roses — red, white, pink, and a deep, almost black crimson that Hadrian had told him was a rare variety cultivated only in the imperial gardens — and then opened out onto the gentle slope that led down to the pond.

*There it is,* Wulfgar thought, and felt his heart lift.

The pond lay before him like a jewel set into the green velvet of the garden — a broad, irregular oval of water, perhaps thirty paces across at its widest point, its surface mirror-still and reflecting the pale morning sky with such fidelity that it was difficult to tell where water ended and air began. The natural spring that fed it emerged from a cluster of mossy rocks at the far end, trickling over a series of small stone ledges with a gentle, musical splashing that was the only sound in the otherwise perfect silence.

The water was clear — extraordinarily clear, with a faintly green tint that came from the profusion of aquatic plants growing on the bottom: long, trailing ribbons of pondweed, feathery clumps of water milfoil, and dense cushions of moss that covered the submerged stones like miniature forests. Through this submarine garden, fish moved — Wulfgar could see them from where he stood, even at this distance. Dark shapes, some large, some small, drifting through the green water with the languid, unhurried movements of creatures that had never known a predator.

*Until now,* some primal part of his brain whispered, and he felt a familiar stirring — the old hunting instinct, the ancestral imperative that no amount of Roman civilization could entirely suppress.

But that was a thought for later. First, the water.

He quickened his pace, his bare feet leaving the gravel path and meeting the soft, dew-wet grass of the bank. The grass was cool and silky between his toes — a sensation so purely pleasurable that it made him gasp slightly, a sharp little intake of breath that was half surprise and half delight. Droplets of dew clung to the golden hair on his shins and calves as he waded through the knee-high grass, and the coolness spread up through his legs like a sweet, refreshing current.

He reached the water's edge and stopped.

The pond was fringed with reeds and rushes — tall, slender stems topped with brown, velvety seed heads that swayed gently in the breeze. Between the reeds, the bank sloped gradually down into the water, the grass giving way first to mud, then to clean sand, then to the submerged stones and plants of the pond bottom. The water lapped gently at the shore, pushed by the faint current from the spring, and its surface was so still and clear near the edges that Wulfgar could see the bottom with perfect clarity — individual grains of sand, the intricate patterns of tiny snail shells, the slow, deliberate progress of a water beetle making its way across a submerged stone.

He put one foot in.

*Cold.* Not unpleasantly so — not the bone-shattering, breath-stealing cold of the Germanic rivers he had grown up swimming in, where the water came straight from snowmelt and could stop a man's heart if he wasn't careful. This was a gentler cold, a Mediterranean cold — bracing, refreshing, alive, but ultimately welcoming. The water closed around his foot and ankle like a cool, liquid glove, and the sensation sent a shiver of pleasure racing up his leg and into his spine.

*Yes,* he thought. *Oh yes. This is what I needed.*

He waded in.

The water rose around him as he advanced — past his ankles, past his calves, past his knees. When it reached his thighs, he sucked in a breath through his teeth — the shock of cold water on warm skin, that exquisite moment of contact that was simultaneously uncomfortable and thrilling. The water continued to climb — past his hips, swallowing the juncture of his thighs with a cold embrace that made him gasp and clench involuntarily, past his waist, lapping at the corrugated surface of his stomach, until finally it reached his chest and he stopped, standing waist-deep in the center of the pond with the water gently undulating around him.

He exhaled slowly, a long, shuddering breath of pure contentment, and let himself sink lower, bending his knees until the water rose to his collarbones, then to his chin. The cold enveloped him completely now — a total, all-encompassing embrace that seemed to dissolve the boundary between his body and the world, to erase the distinction between self and other, between the young man and the water that held him.

*This,* he thought, *is how it felt to be born. This is how the gods intended us to begin each day — immersed in water, clean and cold and new.*

He tilted his head back and let his hair fan out on the surface of the water, spreading around his head like a golden halo. The sun was climbing higher now, clearing the tops of the cypress trees, and its rays fell on his upturned face with a gentle warmth that contrasted deliciously with the cool water embracing the rest of his body. He closed his eyes and floated — or half-floated, his feet still touching the sandy bottom, his body buoyant and weightless, rocking gently with the subtle current.

For several minutes, he simply existed. He did not think about Rome, or the emperor, or the complex web of politics and desire that had brought him to this place. He did not think about his homeland, or his father, or the uncertain future that awaited him. He simply floated in the cool water and felt the sun on his face and listened to the birds singing in the trees and the gentle splashing of the spring and the distant, nearly inaudible hum of the great city beyond the villa's walls.

*I am here,* he thought. *I am alive. I am in water. That is enough. That is everything.*

### Chapter IV: The Hunter's Eye

It was the fish that brought him back.

He had been floating in his blissful, meditative state for perhaps a quarter of an hour when he felt something brush against his leg — a quick, darting touch, like the caress of a cold finger, there and gone in an instant. His eyes snapped open.

A fish. A large carp, by the feel of it — its body smooth and muscular, its movement quick and purposeful. It had been passing by, following whatever inscrutable aquatic agenda fish pursued in their daily lives, and it had grazed his calf in passing, probably mistaking his pale, still leg for a submerged log or a particularly interesting piece of pondweed.

Wulfgar remained perfectly motionless, only his eyes moving as he scanned the water around him. There — another one. A big, handsome carp, easily the length of his forearm, its scales catching the slanting morning light and flashing bronze and gold as it turned. And there — two more, smaller, hovering near the bottom in the shadow of a submerged stone, their fins waving in gentle, rhythmic undulations. And there, near the reeds at the far bank, a whole school of dace — quick, silvery little fish darting in tight formation, turning and wheeling in perfect synchrony as if choreographed by some invisible conductor.

*Fish,* thought Wulfgar, and the word triggered an immediate and powerful chain of associations in his brain — associations that went back to his earliest childhood, to the riverbanks of the Weser, to long summer days spent learning the ancient art of fishing from his uncle Thormod, who was universally acknowledged as the greatest fisherman the Cherusci had ever produced.

*Fish,* he thought again, and this time the word was accompanied by a visceral sensation — a tightening in his stomach, a quickening of his pulse, a sudden sharp awareness of the fact that he had not yet eaten this morning and that his belly was, now that he thought about it, extremely empty.

*Breakfast,* his mind supplied helpfully.

He stood slowly, water streaming off his chest and shoulders, and looked around the pond with new eyes — not the dreamy, contemplative eyes of a young man enjoying a morning swim, but the sharp, calculating eyes of a hunter assessing his prey.

*There are at least a dozen fish in this pond that would make a good meal,* he thought, watching the big carp cruise past him again at a distance of perhaps three arm-lengths. *Fat, lazy, well-fed Roman fish that have never known the danger of net or spear. They would be easy to catch. But how?*

He had no net. He had no spear. He had no fishing line, no hooks, no traps. He was standing naked in a pond with nothing but his bare hands and his wits, and while his hands were large and strong and quick, catching fish with bare hands was a difficult and uncertain business even for the most skilled practitioner. The fish in this pond were fat but not stupid — they would scatter at the first aggressive movement, and chasing them through the water would be an exercise in futility.

*Think,* he commanded himself. *What would Uncle Thormod do?*

And then, rising unbidden from the depths of his memory like a bubble from the bottom of a pond, came the answer.

He almost laughed aloud.

*Of course. The old way. The Cherusci way. The way that Thormod taught me when I was ten years old and too impatient to sit still with a fishing line.*

It was a technique that had been passed down through his tribe for generations beyond counting — so old that no one remembered who had first discovered it, so ancient that it seemed less like a human invention and more like a secret whispered by the water spirits themselves. The Romans, with all their engineering genius and their elaborate fish-farming operations, had no knowledge of it. The Greeks, for all their philosophy and their claims to universal wisdom, had never stumbled upon it. It was a uniquely Germanic technique — crude, inelegant, frankly disgusting by civilized standards, and devastatingly effective.

The principle was simple: certain natural gases, when released into water in sufficient concentration, had a powerful narcotic effect on fish. These gases could stun them, disorient them, and in some cases kill them outright, causing them to float helplessly to the surface where they could be scooped up with ease. Various substances could be used to produce these gases — rotting vegetation, certain mineral deposits, particular types of mud found in river bottoms.

Or, as Wulfgar's ancestors had discovered at some point in the mists of prehistory, one could simply use the gases that the human body produced naturally.

*Thormod always said that the best fisherman carries his equipment with him at all times,* Wulfgar thought, and now he did laugh — a low, rumbling chuckle that sent ripples across the surface of the pond and caused the nearest fish to dart away in alarm.

He felt a stirring in his gut — a deep, internal pressure that had been building gradually since he woke up, the natural accumulation of gases produced by last night's dinner, which had been a characteristically lavish Roman affair featuring lentil soup, roasted cabbage, hard-boiled eggs in garum sauce, and an enormous quantity of bread soaked in olive oil. The Germanic gut, already a formidable engine of fermentation under normal circumstances, had processed this Roman feast through the night, and the result was a considerable reservoir of intestinal gas that was even now pressing insistently against his lower abdomen, demanding release.

*Well,* Wulfgar thought, settling himself more firmly into position, planting his feet wide apart on the sandy bottom and sinking lower into the water until it reached his chest, *if nature provides, it would be rude to refuse.*

He took a moment to assess the tactical situation. The largest concentration of fish — including the big carp and several of his smaller companions — was clustered about four feet to his right, near a submerged log where aquatic plants provided shelter and food. If he could release the gas in a sustained burst and direct the resulting underwater plume toward this cluster, there was a good chance of stunning several fish simultaneously.

*Position is everything,* he recalled Thormod saying, all those years ago on the banks of the Weser, demonstrating the technique with the matter-of-fact practicality that characterized everything the old man did. *You must be deep enough that the bubbles do not simply rise to the surface and dissipate. You want them to spread through the water, to saturate the area around the fish. And you must be still — perfectly still — so the fish do not flee before the gas reaches them.*

Wulfgar adjusted his stance, lowering himself until the water reached his shoulders. He angled his hips slightly, ensuring that the point of release would be well below the waterline. He relaxed his abdominal muscles experimentally, feeling the gas shift and redistribute within his intestines like cargo settling in the hold of a ship.

*This is going to be a big one,* he thought, with a mixture of anticipation and something approaching professional pride. *Last night's lentils have seen to that.*

He took a deep breath. He held it. He looked at the fish — the beautiful, oblivious, soon-to-be-breakfast fish — and whispered a quick, silent prayer to Nerthus, the earth goddess of his people, thanking her for the bounty she was about to provide.

Then he bore down.

### Chapter V: The Technique

The release was monumental.

It began as a deep, rumbling vibration in the very core of his being — a seismic tremor originating somewhere in the labyrinthine depths of his large intestine and traveling outward through his body like the shockwave from a distant earthquake. Wulfgar felt it building, gathering force and momentum as it descended through his gut, and he braced himself, planting his feet even more firmly on the sandy bottom and gripping his own thighs with both hands, his powerful fingers digging into the pale, submerged flesh.

His face underwent a remarkable transformation in the seconds before the release. His ice-blue eyes, normally so calm and observant, widened perceptibly, the pupils dilating. His nostrils flared. His jaw clenched, the muscles along its square line standing out in sharp relief, and a tendon in his neck — thick as a finger — rose beneath the skin as he bore down with his abdominal muscles. His brow furrowed into deep creases, his golden eyebrows drawing together in an expression of intense, focused concentration — the same expression he might have worn when drawing a heavy longbow or wrestling a particularly stubborn opponent. His lips pressed together, then parted slightly, and a low, involuntary grunt escaped from between his teeth — a primal, guttural sound that belonged to the forests and the caves, not to the perfumed gardens of an imperial villa.

His broad chest expanded as he held his breath, the thick pectoral muscles swelling and the golden hair on his sternum standing on end. His abdominal muscles, already well-defined, clenched into a rigid wall of corrugated flesh, each individual segment standing out like the plates of a Roman legionary's lorica segmentata. His powerful buttocks — those twin pale globes of muscle — contracted visibly beneath the water, the gluteal muscles clenching and then, crucially, relaxing as his sphincter opened to permit the passage of what proved to be an extraordinarily substantial volume of gas.

The sound, muffled by the water, was like nothing so much as the distant rumble of thunder — a low, sustained, resonant BRRRRRRUUUUUUUUMMMMMPPPPPHHHHH that seemed to go on for an improbable length of time, vibrating through the water with a physicality that Wulfgar could feel in his very bones. It was not a sharp, staccato bark but rather a long, rolling, almost majestic basso profundo emission that had distinct phases — an initial explosive opening salvo, a sustained middle section of impressive volume and duration, and a gradual, tapering conclusion that trailed off into a series of smaller, staccato aftershocks, like the diminishing echoes of a thunderclap rolling away across a distant plain.

The effect on the water was immediate and dramatic.

A great eruption of bubbles burst from beneath and behind him — not a delicate stream of tiny pearls, but a violent, churning torrent of large, fat, irregular bubbles that roiled the surface of the pond as if it were being heated from below. The water around Wulfgar's midsection seemed to boil, the surface breaking and reforming in chaotic patterns as bubble after bubble — some the size of grapes, some the size of plums, a few approaching the dimensions of small apples — rose from the depths and burst upon the surface with audible, glutinous *plops*. The turbulence spread outward from his body in concentric rings, sending wavelets rippling toward the banks and setting the reeds and rushes swaying as if caught in a sudden wind.

The water itself seemed to change color in the immediate vicinity of the release — taking on a faintly yellowish, murky quality as the gas diffused through the clear water, creating visible currents and eddies that spread outward like ink dropped into a glass. Tendrils of disturbed sediment rose from the pond bottom where the force of the bubbles had disturbed the sand, adding to the general murkiness and giving the water a turbid, almost sulfurous appearance.

Above the surface, where the bubbles were bursting in their dozens, a visible miasma rose — a faint, shimmering distortion of the air, like the heat haze above a sun-baked road, that marked the release of gases too concentrated and too pungent to remain dissolved in the water. The smell — had any observer been close enough to detect it — was extraordinary: a dense, sulfurous, almost weaponized stench that combined the worst elements of rotten eggs, stagnant marshwater, fermented cabbage, and something uniquely and indescribably biological. It was the olfactory equivalent of a siege weapon — concentrated, devastating, and effective at considerable range.

Then it was over.

The last bubbles rose and burst. The turbulence subsided. The murky water began, slowly, to clear. And Wulfgar — Wulfgar stood motionless in the center of the pond, and on his face was an expression of such pure, transcendent relief that it bordered on the religious.

His eyes were half-closed, the lids heavy with a pleasure so fundamental and so complete that it seemed to transcend the merely physical and enter the realm of the spiritual. His lips were parted in a soft, blissful smile — the same drowsy, satisfied smile that might be seen on the face of a man who has just consumed a perfect meal, or completed an act of love, or received news that a long-anticipated wish has been granted. His entire body had relaxed, the tension draining from his muscles like water from a cracked vessel, leaving him loose and languid and profoundly, bone-deeply content. His broad shoulders, which had been bunched and rigid during the effort, had dropped several inches, and his chest rose and fell with the slow, deep rhythm of a man utterly at peace with himself and his world.

"Ohhhhh," he breathed, the sound escaping him involuntarily — a long, shuddering exhalation that was half-sigh, half-groan, entirely animal. "Oh, by the thundering balls of Donar, that was..."

He trailed off, unable to find words in either Germanic or the rudimentary Latin he had acquired sufficient to capture the magnitude of what he had just experienced. It was as if an enormous pressure that he had not even been fully aware of carrying had suddenly been released — as if a great stone had been rolled from the mouth of a cave, allowing light and air to rush in where before there had been only darkness and compression. His entire abdomen felt loose, warm, and pleasantly hollow, like a wineskin that has been emptied of its contents and left to hang slack and unburdened in the breeze.

*That,* he thought, his internal monologue resuming with a tone of deep satisfaction, *was one of the finest farts I have ever produced. If there were competitions for such things — and among the Cherusci, there were, during the winter festivals — that one would have taken the prize. Thormod himself would have been impressed. Father would have been proud.*

He chuckled at this thought, imagining the stern, weather-beaten face of Sigeric breaking into an uncharacteristic grin of paternal approval.

*"Well done, my son,"* the imaginary Sigeric said. *"You are a true Cherusci. Now collect your fish."*

### Chapter VI: The Harvest

Wulfgar did not have to wait long.

The gas, having been released in such impressive volume and concentration, had done its work with brutal efficiency. Within moments of the eruption, Wulfgar began to notice changes in the behavior of the fish around him.

The first sign was the big carp — the one he had been eyeing earlier, the handsome bronze-and-gold specimen that had brushed against his leg. It had been hovering near the submerged log, perhaps four feet from the epicenter of the blast, and now it was behaving strangely. Its movements, previously smooth and purposeful, had become erratic — jerky, uncoordinated, as if the signals from its brain were arriving at its fins garbled and out of sequence. It turned in a tight, dizzy circle, then listed to one side, then righted itself with a visible effort, then listed again. Its gill covers were flapping rapidly, opening and closing with a desperate, panting rhythm that spoke of a creature in acute respiratory distress.

*Come on,* Wulfgar thought, watching with the calm, patient intensity of a born predator. *Come on, my beauty. Just let go. Stop fighting it. Let the water take you.*

As if in response to his silent urging, the carp shuddered — a full-body tremor that traveled from its blunt nose to the very tip of its broad tail — and then, with a slow, almost graceful finality, it rolled onto its side. Its golden eye stared up at the sky, blank and glassy. Its fins twitched once, twice, and were still.

It floated to the surface.

*One,* Wulfgar counted.

More followed in quick succession. Two smaller carp, both about the length of his hand, surfaced together, their pale bellies turned upward, their scales catching the light as they drifted in the gentle current. A fat, dark-backed tench — a species Wulfgar recognized from the rivers of his homeland — bobbed up near the reeds, its barbels trailing limply in the water. Three dace, their silver flanks flashing, broke the surface in a cluster, spinning slowly in the dispersing remnants of the turbulence.

*Two, three, four, five, six, seven,* Wulfgar counted, his grin widening with each new addition to the floating harvest.

He felt a surge of pure, uncomplicated joy — the joy of the hunter, the joy of the provider, the deep, ancestral satisfaction of a man who has used his wits and his body to procure food from the wild. It was a feeling that no Roman banquet, however elaborate, could match — because this food had not been prepared by slaves in a kitchen, had not been purchased with coins in a market, had not been served on golden plates by deferential hands. This food had been won. He had won it. With nothing but his naked body and the ancient wisdom of his people.

*The Romans would be horrified,* he thought gleefully, wading toward the nearest floating fish — the big carp — and reaching out to scoop it from the water. *If they knew how these fish were caught, they would never eat them. They would probably vomit. They would probably pass a law against it.*

He lifted the carp from the water and held it up, examining it with a critical eye. It was a magnificent specimen — easily three pounds, its scales gleaming like hammered gold, its body thick and well-muscled from a life of easy feeding in the emperor's pond. Its flesh would be firm, sweet, and rich with fat.

*You will make excellent eating, my friend,* Wulfgar told the dead fish silently, with the respectful gratitude that his people always showed toward the animals that gave their lives to feed them. *I thank you for your sacrifice. Your death was quick and painless — quicker and more painless than anything you would have experienced in the jaws of a heron or the net of a fisherman. Be at peace.*

He tucked the carp under his arm — an awkward arrangement, given that both man and fish were wet and slippery — and waded toward the next nearest prize, the fat tench by the reeds.

*Seven fish,* he thought as he collected them one by one, cradling them against his bare chest, their cool, smooth bodies pressing against his warm skin. *Seven fish for one fart. That has to be some kind of record. When I die and go to the halls of the ancestors, I will be able to tell this story at the eternal feast, and the heroes of old will raise their mead-horns and salute me.*

He paused, standing waist-deep in the pond with an armload of dead fish, and laughed — a full, rich, booming laugh that sent the birds in the nearest cypress tree erupting into startled flight and echoed off the marble walls of the distant villa.

*Wulfgar the Fish-Slayer,* he thought, still laughing. *Wulfgar Death-Wind. Wulfgar Thunder-Arse, scourge of carp, terror of tench, the man who conquered the emperor's pond with nothing but his own magnificent fundament.*

He began wading toward the bank, his precious cargo clutched against his chest, still chuckling intermittently as new and increasingly ridiculous titles for himself suggested themselves to his imagination.

*They will compose songs about this. They will carve it on runestones. "Here lies Wulfgar, son of Sigeric, who farted so mightily that fish died." It will be my legacy. My immortal contribution to the history of my people.*

He reached the bank and clambered out of the water, his naked body streaming rivulets that caught the sunlight and turned briefly to liquid gold before falling to darken the grass at his feet. He laid the seven fish out in a neat row on the bank — the big golden carp at one end, the three small silver dace at the other, with the two smaller carp and the tench arranged in between — and stood back to admire his catch with his fists planted on his bare, wet hips and his chest swelled with pride.

*Not bad,* he thought, nodding approvingly. *Not bad at all. Enough for a proper meal — more than enough, actually. I could eat three of these and still have four left over. I could share them with Hadrian. I could—*

He paused, considering.

*Actually, perhaps I will not tell Hadrian how I caught them. He is a worldly man and an open-minded one, but there are limits. If he knew that the fish on his plate had been killed by a barbarian's flatulence, it might dampen his appetite. And his affection.*

The thought made him grin again.

*No. I will tell him I caught them by hand. It is not entirely a lie — I did use my hands. To collect them from the surface. After the gas had done its work. It is merely... an incomplete truth. An edited account. The Romans do it all the time — they call it rhetoric.*

### Chapter VII: Fire and Feast

The sun had climbed higher by now, and the garden was filling with warm, golden light. The dew was burning off the grass, rising in faint wisps of mist that gave the landscape an ethereal, dreamlike quality. Somewhere in the villa, Wulfgar could hear the sounds of the household in full swing — voices, footsteps, the clatter of pottery, the distant strains of a flute being practiced by some unseen musician.

*I should dress,* he thought, glancing down at his naked, water-beaded body. *I should go inside, put on a tunic, take these fish to the kitchen, and let the slaves prepare them properly, with olive oil and garum and whatever other Roman sauces they deem necessary.*

But even as the thought formed, he was already rejecting it. The Romans cooked their fish into submission — drowning them in sauces, burying them under spices, baking them in elaborate pastry constructions that bore no discernible relationship to the original animal. Wulfgar wanted none of that. He wanted his fish the way his people had always prepared them — simply, over an open fire, with nothing but flame and smoke to season them.

*I will cook them here,* he decided. *In the garden. Over a fire. The way Thormod taught me.*

There was a small fire pit near the garden's south wall — a circular stone-lined depression that the garden slaves used to burn pruned branches and dead vegetation. It was not an official cooking facility by any means, but it would serve. Wulfgar gathered his fish, carrying them carefully in both arms, and made his way across the garden to the fire pit, still naked, still dripping, still grinning with the irrepressible good humor of a young man who has had a very successful morning.

Finding fuel was easy — there were stacks of dried olive branches and trimmed cypress boughs stored under a lean-to near the garden wall, and Wulfgar helped himself liberally, building a small but competent fire with the practiced ease of someone who had been making fires since childhood. He had no flint or steel, but a quick raid on the garden shed yielded a pottery lamp that still had a flickering flame, and within minutes, a cheerful little blaze was crackling in the fire pit, sending a column of fragrant smoke spiraling up into the morning air.

While the fire burned down to cooking coals, Wulfgar prepared the fish. He had no knife, but his strong, blunt fingernails served well enough for the rough work of gutting and scaling — another skill learned at Thormod's knee, performed now with an almost meditative focus and precision. He sat cross-legged on the warm grass beside the fire pit, his bare skin drying in the sun, and worked his way methodically through the seven fish, opening their bellies with his thumbnail, pulling out their guts with his fingers, and scraping their scales off against the edge of a flat stone.

*This is the best part,* he thought as he worked, his hands slippery with fish blood and viscera, his face serene with concentration. *Not the catching. Not the eating. The preparing. The moment between the hunt and the feast, when you hold the food in your hands and make it ready, when you are connected to the whole ancient chain of actions that has kept our people alive since the beginning of the world. Hunter, preparer, cook, eater. Each step sacred. Each step necessary.*

He skewered the cleaned fish on green sticks cut from an oleander bush — a technique that would have horrified a Roman cook, who would have insisted on proper iron skewers and a well-maintained brazier — and propped them over the bed of glowing coals at a careful angle, adjusting their position with the unconscious expertise of long practice.

The fish began to cook.

The smell was extraordinary — the clean, rich, faintly sweet aroma of fresh fish flesh meeting hot smoke, the sizzle of rendering fat dripping onto coals and sending up little bursts of fragrant steam, the deeper, more complex perfume of the olive-wood embers themselves, with their hints of resin and dried herbs. The skins of the fish tightened and crisped, turning from silver and gold to a deep, burnished brown, and the flesh beneath grew opaque and firm, steaming gently through the splits that the heat had opened along their flanks.

Wulfgar sat beside his fire, naked and golden in the morning sun, tending his fish with patience and care, and he was, in that moment, perfectly and completely happy.

*This is who I am,* he thought, watching the flames dance and the smoke rise and the fish sizzle on their makeshift spits. *Not a courtier. Not a concubine. Not a hostage or a diplomat or a political tool. I am a man sitting by a fire, cooking fish that he caught with his own hands — well, with his own body, at least — and there is no more honest or honorable thing in the world to be.*

He thought of Hadrian then — of the emperor's kind, intelligent face, his neatly trimmed beard shot through with silver, his dark eyes that held such depths of thought and feeling. He thought of the way Hadrian looked at him sometimes — with a mixture of desire and tenderness and something almost like sadness, as if he were looking at something beautiful that he knew he could not keep forever.

*He loves me,* Wulfgar thought simply. *In his way, as much as a Roman emperor can love anyone. And I... I care for him. Truly. He is a good man — better than most Romans, better than many of my own people. He treats me with respect. He listens when I speak. He does not try to change me or tame me. He lets me be what I am.*

He turned the fish, exposing their other sides to the heat.

*But he does not understand this,* Wulfgar continued, gesturing vaguely at the fire, the fish, the pond, the garden, his own naked body — the whole scene of primitive self-sufficiency playing out in the heart of the world's greatest empire. *He does not understand that this — this simple thing, this cooking of fish over a fire — is what makes me happy. Not the silk sheets or the golden plates or the marble floors. This.*

The first fish was ready. Wulfgar lifted it from the coals and examined it critically — the skin was perfectly crisped, the flesh firm and flaky, the aroma almost unbearably enticing. He blew on it twice to cool it, then bit into it directly, tearing a large chunk of hot, succulent flesh from the bone with his strong white teeth.

The flavor was superb — clean, sweet, delicate, with a faint smokiness from the olive-wood coals and a richness that spoke of the pond's abundant food supply. The flesh melted on his tongue, releasing a burst of savory juice that was so purely and perfectly delicious that Wulfgar actually closed his eyes and moaned — a low, rumbling sound of gastronomic ecstasy that was remarkably similar to the sounds he sometimes made in Hadrian's bed, though the emperor would probably not have appreciated the comparison.

*Oh, that is good,* he thought, chewing blissfully. *That is very, very good. Thank you, Nerthus. Thank you, fish. Thank you, lentils that I ate for dinner last night, without which this magnificent catch would never have been possible.*

He ate the first fish in four enormous bites, consuming everything — flesh, skin, and the small, crunchy bones, which he chewed and swallowed with evident relish. Then he reached for the second fish, and the third, devouring them with the focused, single-minded appetite of a young man who has been swimming in cold water on an empty stomach and has just cooked himself the freshest meal of his life.

By the time he had finished the fourth fish, his appetite was satisfied, and he leaned back on his elbows in the warm grass, his belly full, his skin dry and sun-warmed, his face and fingers greasy with fish oil. The remaining three fish still sat on their skewers beside the fire, their flesh cooling and firming in the morning air.

*Those I will save,* he decided. *For dinner. I will bring them to Hadrian and say, "I caught these for you in your pond. I caught them with my hands." And he will smile and be pleased, because he loves it when I do things that remind him I am not Roman, that I come from a different world.*

*And if he asks how I caught them — how I really caught them — I will smile and say nothing. Some secrets are best kept between a man and his pond.*

He lay back fully in the grass, spreading his arms wide, staring up at the great blue dome of the Italian sky, and he smiled — a wide, free, unreserved smile that transformed his bold, angular face into something radiant and young and utterly alive.

*Not a bad morning,* thought Wulfgar, son of Sigeric, of the Cherusci. *Not a bad morning at all.*

Somewhere in the villa, a bell rang, signaling the start of the emperor's midday audiences. Slaves scurried, senators gathered, the vast machinery of empire ground on with its relentless, meticulous efficiency.

And in the garden, naked in the sun, a young barbarian lay beside a dying fire and the remnants of his fish and was, for a perfect, suspended moment, the happiest man in Rome.

# Peak Element - Binary Search Solution in Elixir

## Approach

We use binary search to achieve O(log n) time complexity. The key insight is:
- If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, then a peak must exist on the right side (mid + 1 to right)
- Otherwise, a peak must exist on the left side (left to mid, inclusive)

This works because of the boundary condition where `nums[-1] = nums[n] = -∞`.

## Solution

```elixir
defmodule Solution do
  @spec find_peak_element(nums :: [integer]) :: integer
  def find_peak_element(nums) do
    nums_tuple = List.to_tuple(nums)
    n = tuple_size(nums_tuple)
    binary_search(nums_tuple, 0, n - 1)
  end

  defp binary_search(_nums, left, right) when left == right do
    left
  end

  defp binary_search(nums, left, right) do
    mid = div(left + right, 2)

    if elem(nums, mid) < elem(nums, mid + 1) do
      binary_search(nums, mid + 1, right)
    else
      binary_search(nums, left, mid)
    end
  end
end
```

## Explanation

1. **Convert list to tuple**: Since Elixir lists have O(n) random access, we convert to a tuple first to get O(1) access via `elem/2`.

2. **Binary search logic**:
   - **Base case**: When `left == right`, we've narrowed down to a single element — this is a peak.
   - **Recursive case**: 
     - Calculate `mid = (left + right) / 2`
     - If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`: the slope is increasing, so a peak must be to the right → search `[mid + 1, right]`
     - Otherwise: `nums[mid] >= nums[mid + 1]`, so a peak is at `mid` or to the left → search `[left, mid]`

3. **Why this works**: Since `nums[i] != nums[i+1]` for all valid `i`, and boundaries are `-∞`, there's always guaranteed to be a peak. By always moving toward the "uphill" direction, we're guaranteed to find one.

## Complexity

- **Time**: O(log n) — standard binary search
- **Space**: O(log n) for recursion stack (could be O(1) with iterative approach)

## Example Walkthrough

For `nums = [1, 2, 3, 1]`:
- left=0, right=3, mid=1: nums[1]=2 < nums[2]=3 → search right [2, 3]
- left=2, right=3, mid=2: nums[2]=3 > nums[3]=1 → search left [2, 2]
- left=2, right=2 → return **2** ✓

```python
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse


class WebPageScraper:
    """Scrapes a web page for title, keywords, description, and URLs."""

    def __init__(self, url, timeout=10):
        self.url = url
        self.timeout = timeout
        self.soup = None
        self.html = None

    def download_page(self):
        """Download the web page content."""
        try:
            headers = {
                'User-Agent': ('Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) '
                               'AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) '
                               'Chrome/91.0.4472.124 Safari/537.36')
            }
            response = requests.get(
                self.url,
                headers=headers,
                timeout=self.timeout
            )
            response.raise_for_status()  # Raise exception for HTTP errors
            self.html = response.text
            self.soup = BeautifulSoup(self.html, 'html.parser')
            print(f"✅ Successfully downloaded: {self.url}")
            print(f"   Status Code: {response.status_code}")
            print(f"   Content Length: {len(self.html)} characters")
            return True

        except requests.exceptions.MissingSchema:
            print(f"❌ Invalid URL format: {self.url}")
        except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
            print(f"❌ Failed to connect to: {self.url}")
        except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
            print(f"❌ Request timed out for: {self.url}")
        except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as e:
            print(f"❌ HTTP Error: {e}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"❌ Unexpected error: {e}")

        return False

    def get_title(self):
        """Extract the page title."""
        if not self.soup:
            return None

        # Method 1: <title> tag
        title_tag = self.soup.find('title')
        if title_tag and title_tag.string:
            return title_tag.string.strip()

        # Method 2: Open Graph title
        og_title = self.soup.find('meta', property='og:title')
        if og_title and og_title.get('content'):
            return og_title['content'].strip()

        # Method 3: First <h1> tag as fallback
        h1_tag = self.soup.find('h1')
        if h1_tag:
            return h1_tag.get_text(strip=True)

        return None

    def get_keywords(self):
        """Extract meta keywords."""
        if not self.soup:
            return []

        # Method 1: Standard meta keywords
        meta_keywords = self.soup.find('meta', attrs={'name': 'keywords'})
        if not meta_keywords:
            # Try case-insensitive search
            meta_keywords = self.soup.find(
                'meta',
                attrs={'name': lambda x: x and x.lower() == 'keywords'}
            )

        if meta_keywords and meta_keywords.get('content'):
            keywords = meta_keywords['content']
            return [kw.strip() for kw in keywords.split(',') if kw.strip()]

        return []

    def get_description(self):
        """Extract meta description."""
        if not self.soup:
            return None

        # Method 1: Standard meta description
        meta_desc = self.soup.find('meta', attrs={'name': 'description'})
        if not meta_desc:
            meta_desc = self.soup.find(
                'meta',
                attrs={'name': lambda x: x and x.lower() == 'description'}
            )

        if meta_desc and meta_desc.get('content'):
            return meta_desc['content'].strip()

        # Method 2: Open Graph description
        og_desc = self.soup.find('meta', property='og:description')
        if og_desc and og_desc.get('content'):
            return og_desc['content'].strip()

        return None

    def get_urls(self, internal_only=False, external_only=False):
        """
        Extract all URLs from the page.

        Args:
            internal_only: Return only internal links
            external_only: Return only external links

        Returns:
            dict with categorized URLs
        """
        if not self.soup:
            return {'internal': [], 'external': [], 'all': []}

        base_domain = urlparse(self.url).netloc
        internal_urls = set()
        external_urls = set()

        for link in self.soup.find_all('a', href=True):
            href = link['href'].strip()

            # Skip empty, javascript, and anchor-only links
            if not href or href.startswith(('#', 'javascript:', 'mailto:', 'tel:')):
                continue

            # Convert relative URLs to absolute
            absolute_url = urljoin(self.url, href)

            # Validate URL
            parsed = urlparse(absolute_url)
            if parsed.scheme not in ('http', 'https'):
                continue

            # Categorize as internal or external
            if parsed.netloc == base_domain:
                internal_urls.add(absolute_url)
            else:
                external_urls.add(absolute_url)

        result = {
            'internal': sorted(internal_urls),
            'external': sorted(external_urls),
            'all': sorted(internal_urls | external_urls)
        }

        if internal_only:
            return result['internal']
        if external_only:
            return result['external']

        return result

    def get_all_metadata(self):
        """Extract all metadata at once."""
        return {
            'url': self.url,
            'title': self.get_title(),
            'description': self.get_description(),
            'keywords': self.get_keywords(),
            'urls': self.get_urls()
        }

    def print_report(self):
        """Print a formatted report of all extracted data."""
        data = self.get_all_metadata()

        print("\n" + "=" * 70)
        print("📄 WEB PAGE ANALYSIS REPORT")
        print("=" * 70)

        # URL
        print(f"\n🔗 URL: {data['url']}")

        # Title
        print(f"\n📌 Title: {data['title'] or 'Not found'}")

        # Description
        desc = data['description']
        if desc:
            # Truncate long descriptions for display
            display_desc = desc[:200] + "..." if len(desc) > 200 else desc
            print(f"\n📝 Description: {display_desc}")
        else:
            print("\n📝 Description: Not found")

        # Keywords
        keywords = data['keywords']
        if keywords:
            print(f"\n🏷️  Keywords ({len(keywords)}):")
            for kw in keywords:
                print(f"   • {kw}")
        else:
            print("\n🏷️  Keywords: Not found")

        # URLs
        urls = data['urls']
        print(f"\n🔗 URLs Found:")
        print(f"   Internal: {len(urls['internal'])}")
        print(f"   External: {len(urls['external'])}")
        print(f"   Total:    {len(urls['all'])}")

        # Show first 10 internal URLs
        if urls['internal']:
            print(f"\n   📁 Internal URLs (showing first 10):")
            for url in urls['internal'][:10]:
                print(f"      → {url}")
            if len(urls['internal']) > 10:
                print(f"      ... and {len(urls['internal']) - 10} more")

        # Show first 10 external URLs
        if urls['external']:
            print(f"\n   🌐 External URLs (showing first 10):")
            for url in urls['external'][:10]:
                print(f"      → {url}")
            if len(urls['external']) > 10:
                print(f"      ... and {len(urls['external']) - 10} more")

        print("\n" + "=" * 70)


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Usage Examples
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def main():
    # Example 1: Basic usage
    url = "https://www.example.com"
    scraper = WebPageScraper(url)

    if scraper.download_page():
        scraper.print_report()

    # Example 2: Get specific data programmatically
    print("\n\n--- Programmatic Access Example ---\n")

    url2 = "https://www.python.org"
    scraper2 = WebPageScraper(url2)

    if scraper2.download_page():
        # Access individual fields
        title = scraper2.get_title()
        print(f"Title: {title}")

        description = scraper2.get_description()
        print(f"Description: {description}")

        keywords = scraper2.get_keywords()
        print(f"Keywords: {keywords}")

        # Get only external URLs
        external = scraper2.get_urls(external_only=True)
        print(f"External URLs count: {len(external)}")

        # Get all metadata as dictionary (useful for JSON/database storage)
        metadata = scraper2.get_all_metadata()
        print(f"\nFull metadata keys: {list(metadata.keys())}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
